result:
**Answer: $[1,\infty)$**, with the caveat that the lower endpoint is justified only by the upper bound below, not by a sharpness construction.

**Why $p\ge 1$ works.** Every finite subfamily of the $g_j$ is a set of at most $m+1$ linearly independent linear forms in $f_0,\dots,f_m$, hence in general position. The Cartan defect relation for linearly nondegenerate entire curves gives, for any finite such subfamily $S$,
$$\sum_{j\in S}\delta_j\le m+1.$$
Since the $\delta_j\in[0,1]$ are nonnegative, letting $S$ grow gives $\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_j\le m+1<\infty$. Because $\delta_j\in[0,1]$, $\delta_j^p\le\delta_j$ for $p\ge1$, so $\sum_j\delta_j^p<\infty$ for every $p\ge1$.

**Why the set cannot be larger in general.** Since $\delta^p$ is decreasing in $p$ on $[0,1]$, the admissible set is an up-set, so the question is whether some $p<1$ also works universally. I did not establish this. The natural candidate counterexample would be a tuple with $\delta_j\sim 1/(j\log^2 j)$, for which $\sum\delta_j^p$ diverges for every $p<1$. I have not verified that such defect sequences are realizable by a linearly nondegenerate $F$ of finite order with general-position $(a_j)$. I also could not recall a published sharper exponent, so the lower endpoint rests on the sum bound together with the expectation that the bound is sharp.

ANSWER: $[1,\infty)$
